title: Where? Where to?
title_target: Хаана байна вэ? Хаашаа явж байна вэ?
goal: Naming places — and mastering the suffix *-д / -т*, one suffix that does the job of three English prepositions at once: in/at, to, and toward.
bekal: say where something is and where you are going
ask for directions in the city and understand the answer

dialogs.title: Яриа — Сүхбаатарын талбай хаана вэ?
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost in downtown Ulaanbaatar. He asks a woman at a bus stop.

notes: ⚠️ **One suffix, three English prepositions.** *Сургуульд* can mean "**at** school", "**to** school", or "**toward** the school". What decides is not the suffix but **the verb**: *байна* (to be) → "at"; *явна* (go) → "to"; *хэлнэ* (say) → "to (someone)". It saves a lot of memorizing, but it means reading the sentence to the end before you translate.

**Хаана = where, хаашаа = where to, хаанаас = where from.** All three grow from *хаа*, and their suffixes are the same as on ordinary nouns. The same pattern works for *энд/ийшээ/эндээс* and *тэнд/тийшээ/тэндээс*.

**Байгаа is not just another form of байна.** *Байна* states a present situation; *байгаа* is a "hanging" form, used when asking whether something exists (*Банк байгаа юу?* — Is there a bank?) or to describe a noun. For now, learn *байгаа юу?* as one ready-made chunk: "is there …?"

**Их сургууль literally means "big school" and means university.** This pattern is common: *их дэлгүүр* (department store), *их эмч* (head doctor). ⚠️ Don't mix it up with *том*, which also means big — *их* is for abstract size and degree, *том* for physical size.

**The suffix -аар / -ээр on замаар and автобусаар means "along" and "by".** *Замаар* = along the road; *автобусаар* = by bus; *монголоор* = in Mongolian. This suffix gets full treatment in unit 10; just recognize its shape here.

grammars.title: The place suffix: when -д, when -т
body: After *байна*, this is the suffix you will use most. Its two forms are chosen purely by **the sound of the last letter** of the base word — not by vowel group.

head: Word ends in
Suffix
Example
Meaning
rows: *в, г, р, с* and long vowels

after: ⚠️ Row four shows something important: for things with a **surface**, Mongolians don't use the place suffix alone but add a position word (*дээр*, *дотор*). *Ширээд* sounds wrong; *ширээн дээр* is right.

If you pick *-д* instead of *-т*, nobody will misunderstand you. It's a slip on the level of saying "in the weekend" instead of "on the weekend" — slightly off, nothing more. **Don't put off speaking to memorize this table.**

grammars.title: Position words: дээр, дотор, доор, дэргэд
body: English puts "on" **before** the noun. Mongolian puts it **after** — and that is the only difference you need to remember.

Meaning
Example
rows: *хотын **дунд*** — in the middle of the city

after: ⚠️ Notice that the noun changes shape before the position word: *ширээ* → *ширээ**н***, *цүнх* → *цүнх**эн***, *банк* → *банк**ны***, *гэр* → *гэр**ийн***. Some take the possessive suffix (*-ын/-ийн*), some take a hidden *-н*. At A1, just copy the pattern from the examples; the system becomes clear at A2.

**Өмнө has two meanings at once: "in front of" (place) and "before" (time).** *Сургуулийн өмнө* = in front of the school; *хоолны өмнө* = before the meal. English does the same with "before" ("before the king", "before dinner"), so this is nothing strange.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Гэр* is one of the most important words in Mongolian and means both **home** and the **round traditional tent** the outside world often calls a "yurt". Mongolians themselves never use the word "yurt" — it's a Turkic word that came through Russian. If you're invited to someone's *гэрт*, you're invited to their home, whatever shape it has.

blocks.title: Four direction words you must know
items: ⚠️ This system assumes you are **facing south** — an old habit from the ger door, which always faces south. That is why "right" is west and "front" is south. It sounds odd until you stand in front of a ger; after that, it makes sense for life.

English
rows: Should I just take a taxi?

blocks.text: That last sentence — *Би төөрчихлөө* — is worth memorizing before you land in Ulaanbaatar. The city has no consistent street names; even locals give addresses by landmarks ("behind shop X, across from stop Y"). If you say you're lost, a Mongolian will very likely not just point the way but walk you there.

blocks.title: Answering "is there …?"
items: *Ойролцоо банк байгаа юу?* — Is there a bank near here?
⚠️ *Байхгүй* is the opposite of *байна* and one of the words you'll hear most in shops and markets: "there isn't", "sold out", "don't have".
*Мэдэхгүй.* — I don't know. Also very common, and not considered rude.
The book is on the table.
The shop is next to the bank.
